Oct 21, 2026

## **decoupled consensus: staggered single committee vs multiple committees**

Invited [Sukun Tarachandani](mailto:sukun.tarachandani@ethereum.org) [mikhail.kalinin@consensys.com](mailto:mikhail.kalinin@consensys.com) [Ben Edgington](mailto:ben.edgington@ethereum.org) [Roberto Saltini](mailto:roberto.saltini@ethereum.org) [Yann Vonlanthen](mailto:yann.vonlanthen@ethereum.org) [anton.nashatyrev@consensys.com](mailto:anton.nashatyrev@consensys.com) [Kamil Salakhiev](mailto:kamil.salakhiev@ethereum.org)

Attachments [decoupled consensus: staggered single committee vs multiple committees](https://calendar.google.com/calendar/event?eid=MTdvcWs1dmtlcjdtODQ4amk0aHYwc2hkMHEgc3VrdW4udGFyYWNoYW5kYW5pQGV0aGVyZXVtLm9yZw)

Meeting records [Transcript](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1qzwJU3XlBJiGPvaPtz6LI_6K7jgXio3THsG1UK4_4KI/edit?usp=drive_web&tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at) 

### **Summary**

Subnet voting strategies debated and bandwidth requirements evaluated for optimal network resilience.

**Subnet Voting Strategies**  
Evaluation of heterogeneous slot structures versus decoupled homogeneous voting mechanisms.

**Bandwidth and Slot Comparisons**  
Analysis of network load and bandwidth requirements for different sub-round approaches.

**Specification and Prioritization**  
Prioritization constraints discussed and baseline specification delivery established as primary priority.

### **Decisions**

## Needs Further Discussion

* **Voting strategy structural architecture** The group evaluated heterogeneous sub-round versus homogeneous decoupled slot voting strategies but deferred final alignment to investigate hybrid dimensional design options.

* **Bit list encoding schema design** Participants deliberated on creating an efficient bit list encoding schema independent of aggregation topology while acknowledging that further investigation is required.

## Aligned

* **Adopting the default staggering solution for specification** The team aligned on adopting the default solution of staggering for the specification as soon as possible while continuing to think about and outline desired properties.

### **Next steps**

- [ ] \[Sukun, Mikhail\] Research Encoding Schema: Develop a bit list encoding schema that is independent of aggregation topology. Ensure the encoding remains efficient and simple enough for state transitions.

- [ ] \[The group\] Implement Topic Prioritization: Design topic prioritization to ensure goldfish votes are delivered promptly despite other network traffic. Incorporate this mechanism to improve protocol robustness.

- [ ] \[Sukun Tarachandani\] Run simulation: Run a simulation to evaluate the impact of goldfish vote overlap in the proposed voting schemes.

- [ ] \[The group\] Spec approaches: Draft specifications for both staggered and sub-round voting approaches to analyze their implementation complexity.

- [ ] \[The group\] Define Properties: Consider the desired properties for the proposed solutions.

- [ ] \[Yann Vonlanthen\] Update Documentation: Refine the current documentation and notify the team when it is ready for review.

- [ ] \[Sukun Tarachandani\] Draft Properties: Draft a document detailing property requirements to compare against existing models.

- [ ] \[Kamil Salakhiev\] Push Prioritization: Introduce networking forks to initiate the prioritization implementation.

- [ ] \[The group\] Schedule Discussion: Convene next Tuesday to continue the discussion regarding the proposed solutions.

### **Details**

**Agenda and Voting Strategies**: Sukun Tarachandani shared slides in the repository and outlined the meeting agenda to discuss two voting strategies for subnets ([00:00:49](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.fcg2xb1fne93)). The first strategy involves a heterogeneous slot structure with one committee per subnet every slot, featuring attestation votes initially and aggregate votes toward the end. The second strategy is more homogeneous and decoupled, allowing votes and aggregates to flow continuously throughout the slot without heterogeneity ([00:04:19](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.yozic3w6gsfr)).

![][image1]

---

**Sub-Round Voting Structure Mechanics**: Sukun Tarachandani explained that in the first strategy, approximately one-seventh of a committee (around 300 voters out of 2,000 total) votes at every second interval, sending one aggregate at the 9-second mark, though these numbers can be adjusted. Roberto Saltini and Sukun Tarachandani clarified that all seven groups use the same subnet, and all 16 aggregators for the subnet contribute to a single global topic aggregate containing votes from all groups ([00:05:43](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.ze2ik76bculh)). Sukun Tarachandani renamed this "multiple committees" approach to "sub-rounds" because distinct sub-rounds occur at every point in the slot ([00:07:01](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.yjn6gqaoado5)). Mikhail noted that aggregators from committee 3 could technically aggregate attestations from committees 1 and 2 if desired, since committee indices are not strictly signed into attestation data ([00:10:53](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.33j5vtv1sgeo)).

![][image2]

---

**Bit List Encoding and Topology Independence**: Mikhail raised questions about encoding schemas for validator indices and bit lists, pointing out that today's committee-based mapping leaks the aggregation topology into the validator bit encoding ([00:12:03](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.bcejhy5hfzwz)) ([00:14:45](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.h68m4sg8pmeh)). Sukun Tarachandani noted an existing alternative of sending two bit lists—one specifying included committees and a second containing a concatenation of those committees—which avoids including all validator indices ([00:13:32](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.2fkixuyvqamd)). Mikhail argued that an ideal encoding schema should not depend on the aggregation topology, allowing decoding straight from an attestation without requiring epoch inputs, though acknowledging this is difficult to implement ([00:15:55](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.1rosoy57sowt)) ([00:20:47](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.2139pkbr1k93)). Sukun Tarachandani and Yann Vonlanthen discussed potential lossy or lossless compression techniques and the challenge of balancing 30% Byzantine fault tolerance assumptions with network efficiency ([00:18:12](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.1a8sfx3ddnkp)).

![][image3]

---

**Post-Quantum Considerations and Slot Pipelining**: Sukun Tarachandani noted that the sub-round design maps better to post-quantum requirements because it naturally incorporates a delay of one extra sub-round before inclusion, such as votes in sub-round 3 going to a slot after sub-round 5 ([00:20:47](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.2139pkbr1k93)). Kamil Salakhiev and Sukun Tarachandani discussed how this structure allows shrinking slot sizes while increasing vote propagation and aggregation durations, keeping compute-sensitive post-quantum operations pipelined and parallelized across non-overlapping aggregators ([00:22:06](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.pmmx2gt931mc)). Mikhail and Sukun Tarachandani also discussed sub-round sizing, noting that smaller committees avoid congestion without needing strict internal staggering ([00:24:18](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.hfkadz9e0np5)).

---

**Slot Timing, Traffic Prioritization, and Goldfish Safety**: Roberto Saltini expressed concern that without traffic prioritization, finality gadget vote traffic could congest the network and negatively impact goldfish safety, which relies on goldfish votes arriving reliably across the entire slot ([00:27:48](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.7y7zdsd63lu4)). Mikhail agreed that staggering votes acts as an application-layer prioritization method, but noted that scheduling adjustments are required whenever available chain pipeline schedules change ([00:29:00](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.y419vhma685b)). Kamil Salakhiev suggested that prioritization could be introduced later as an optimization between forks since it does not require consensus changes, though Roberto Saltini countered that prioritization makes the protocol fundamentally more robust ([00:32:25](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.n1yppdi4nxx)).

![][image4]

---

**Slot Comparisons and Bandwidth Requirements**: Sukun Tarachandani presented bandwidth calculations showing that a subsystem with 625 members would consume approximately 9.3 megabits per second for the first approach and 8.4 megabits per second for the second approach, assuming a raw gossip factor of 5 derived from x-ray data ([00:39:05](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.cr6jzm52kw0v)) ([00:47:09](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.58j3sfjj9c5i)). Sukun Tarachandani noted that while these requirements might challenge nodes limited to 20 megabits per second during block traffic, they work fine if 20% of the network consists of super nodes or if a 100-megabit per second minimum is established ([00:40:44](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.iq22jl8xbu1m)). Anton Nashatyrev and Sukun Tarachandani clarified that weakest nodes subscribe to only two attestation subnets, whereas aggregates are published on a global topic across all 64 subnets ([00:43:12](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.8nhqr0rbzccb)). Furthermore, Sukun Tarachandani pointed out that super nodes running at home peak at roughly 125 to 200 megabits per second according to conversations with Dustin Traglia ([00:44:21](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.iolhrwfby7kv)).

![][image5]

---

**Aggregate Overlap and Design Trade-Offs**: Mikhail asked whether the staggered approach results in more overlapping aggregates, to which Sukun Tarachandani responded that the staggered method likely allows better aggregation due to having the final 3 seconds completely unconstrained ([00:48:30](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.211vlkdlcvhm)). Yann Vonlanthen suggested viewing the two proposed slot options as separate dimensions—such as pipelining versus no pipelining, continuous aggregation versus end-of-slot aggregation, and enforced vote timing versus flexibility—allowing the team to mix and match the best aspects of both approaches ([00:49:55](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.51yxdi2jsx1t)). Roberto Saltini discussed validator incentives regarding early versus late voting and target progress, while Sukun Tarachandani and Mikhail debated whether decoupled sub-rounds without slot dependency or staggered voting provide a superior architectural model ([00:52:31](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.5rzgjg4bxjct)).

![][image6]

---

**Staggered Voting versus Sub-Round Approaches**: Mikhail opened the discussion by evaluating whether block proposers should aggregate attestations themselves and stagger votes until the end of the slot to mimic a sub-round approach. Mikhail noted that only proposers subscribed to all subnets would participate ([01:00:16](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.afhgc9vlu5ob)). Sukun Tarachandani noted that this equates the sub-round length to a slot with one committee per subnet, and asked why two committees per person could not be used. Mikhail and Roberto Saltini stated they saw no fundamental downside other than tighter time frames, and neither expressed opposition to exploring both options ([01:01:36](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.g12syatv3d4l)).

![][image7]

---

**Bandwidth and Network Resilience under Poor Conditions**: Sukun Tarachandani argued that sub-round systems lack a dedicated space for pushing aggregates only, whereas staggered approaches benefit bandwidth because they do not compete with other tasks ([01:02:52](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.28y2kjlpsen6)). Mikhail noted that at full network capacity, the sub-round approach is more restrictive due to its shorter time frame, potentially forcing reliance on proposers to aggregate late attestations. Kamil Salakhiev inquired about worst-case network conditions, and Mikhail explained that votes would experience delays, requiring proposers in slot n plus one to handle aggregation to prevent losing attestations ([01:04:21](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.m9eqwkcprqou)).

---

**Optimizing Aggregation Schedules and Pipelining**: Roberto Saltini suggested staggering aggregates so they are not all sent simultaneously, thereby reducing peak load risks. Mikhail and Anton Nashatyrev discussed starting aggregation earlier and finishing based on bit field numbers or deadlines, such as the first quarter of the next slot ([01:07:08](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.srvbp3k0qa9h)). Yann Vonlanthen proposed extending the committee aggregation window (C1) to the end of the slot, allowing proposers to continuously improve aggregates while local aggregators publish early to avoid missing out ([01:08:36](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.9n2o5j4sixuy)). Sukun Tarachandani added that participants could be allowed to vote up to a slot late ([01:11:18](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.eptqv48gpswh)).

---

**Implementation Complexity and Baseline Solutions**: Mikhail discussed overlap issues when starting aggregates late in a staggered approach ([01:12:28](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.904m0oauu00b)). Yann Vonlanthen emphasized the importance of pipelining given the busy middle of the slot, while Anton Nashatyrev pointed out that 8 slots per epoch provide ample spare bandwidth, though shorter epochs would necessitate improvements ([01:13:54](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.jrfpu5d9ey46)). Anton argued that the sub-round approach is simpler and more battle-tested because it mirrors existing designs. Mikhail observed that the staggered approach is more relaxed due to its larger time frame ([01:18:09](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.nw8bjlr5ixgs)).

---

**Chain Stability and Prioritization Constraints**: Roberto Saltini emphasized the necessity of prioritization for the stability of the available chain, noting that the second part of a slot is computationally heavy due to execution layer payload processing and propagation. Mikhail agreed that the first part of the slot is crucial for payload and blob column propagation ([01:22:21](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.wrwccwbr5zvu)) ([01:24:47](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.79e064t307i7)). Yann Vonlanthen suggested that the second approach is more future-proof for shorter slots (such as 3-second slots), whereas the first approach is simpler for a single fork ([01:26:05](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.3jhfvqd2rcaj)).

---

**Aesthetic Arguments and Network Load Balancing**: Sukun Tarachandani raised the aesthetic argument that the second approach maintains a steady rate for Friendly Finality Gadget votes. Roberto Saltini expressed concern over goldfish votes and the lack of prioritization, noting that sub-round network loads balance finality but not the available chain ([01:27:17](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.7g7qasijti8p)). Anton Nashatyrev suggested allowing aggregators to aggregate more than once if they receive additional votes after their best aggregate, acknowledging that this could double aggregate traffic in the worst case ([01:28:48](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.qu5a38h2olfl)).

---

**Defining Core Properties and Simulation Results**: Mikhail raised the question of whether to formalize two or three core properties to guide optimization ([01:30:39](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.ezp6khir4ije)). Yann Vonlanthen mentioned starting a document listing properties but favored time-boxing the decision ([01:32:32](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.lnygeh1oiflj)). Sukun Tarachandani noted that with EIP 8334 or snappy compression, doing nothing and keeping epochs at 8 slots would function correctly ([01:33:58](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.98z12sle7ic6)). Sukun shared simulation results comparing staggering without partial messages (Scenario 1\) and with partial messages (Scenario 2), showing that goldfish vote latency remains within 1 second even in worst-case conditions because the network is not at capacity ([01:37:19](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.bupogxu22z7c)).

![][image8]

---

**Refining Sub-Round Intervals and Propagation Windows**: Yann Vonlanthen and Sukun Tarachandani discussed starting sub-rounds every 2 or 3 seconds, noting that traffic is lowest at the start and end of a committee, with peak propagation occurring between 500 milliseconds and 1.5 seconds ([01:38:53](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.x5f3x54686h0)). Mikhail questioned whether to reserve a 1-second buffer for degraded network conditions by spacing intervals to 3 seconds. Sukun suggested a 4-second structure with overlapping first and last two seconds of committees, though Mikhail pointed out that this delays the start of best-case aggregation ([01:40:13](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.9jh22ij44l1y)).

![][image9]

---

**Establishing Specifications versus Defining Protocol Properties**: Yann Vonlanthen argued that waiting to agree on properties before writing a specification is unrealistic given schedule pressures. Mikhail agreed that delivering a baseline specification as soon as possible is the primary priority, even if it is imperfect and subject to later experimentation ([01:42:35](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.cvrq1bkafzdw)). Yann presented two potential paths: an ambitious solution combining pipelining and late aggregation, and a non-ambitious solution mirroring current behavior while relying on gossip-sub prioritization ([01:45:08](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.steld9es5fj2)).

---

**Decoupling Friendly Finality Gadget Votes and Fairness Concerns**: Yann Vonlanthen and Mikhail expressed a preference for decoupling Friendly Finality Gadget votes from slot structures ([01:47:25](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.w6pn4d57wc2j)). Roberto Saltini warned that decoupling risks sacrificing proposer reward fairness, which could provoke strong opinions among participants. Sukun Tarachandani argued that if Friendly Finality Gadget throughput remains stable over 12 seconds, fairness should be maintained ([01:49:20](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.4dx4o5urtgnm)). Roberto requested parameter-bound flexibility to allow switching between staggered and sub-round mechanics to account for future slot length changes ([01:22:21](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.wrwccwbr5zvu)) ([01:50:45](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.1esszgld90te)).

---

**Next Steps on Prioritization and Scheduling**: Sukun Tarachandani asked how to handle message prioritization for aggregators and whether to make it a requirement for headliner proposers. Kamil Salakhiev asked if they could start pushing prioritization immediately, to which Sukun agreed ([01:53:55](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.aluccebquei1)). Roberto Saltini raised concerns about whether partial node implementation of prioritization poses risks and whether it should be bundled into the capital consensus EIP ([01:55:49](?tab=t.ywwh3yjfr6at#heading=h.yqy82d7eevjh)). Yann Vonlanthen thanked participants and scheduled the next follow-up discussion for Tuesday of the following week .
